content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper addresses the slot random initialization problem by applying a conditional clustering algorithm to estimate several clusters (where the number of clusters is estimated with the mean-shift algorithm) based
on the input image information and
initialize the slot representations with the input cluster representations.
The authors verify the effectiveness of the proposed approach over multiple baselines on object discovery and novel view synthesis tasks. 

According to my understanding, the mentioned slot initialization problem is very similar to the object query initialization problem within DETR[1] for object detection.
The key difference is that DETR chooses a learned per-element initialization scheme while slot attention samples the query from a shared learnable Gaussian distribution,
where both approaches can not adjust the query according to different input image contents.
The DETR community has already verified that a content-aware initialization of the object query can accelerate convergence and improves performance. For example, the well-known
Deformable-DETR[2] proposed applying prediction heads on all the pixel features and then selecting the most confident pixel features to act as the initialization
of the object query.
Typically, a better initialization might accelerate the convergence but can not improve the performance upper bound.
So, the authors should report the performance of the original random initialization scheme under longer training schedules or stacking the slot modules more times, where we can treat the proposed method
as an improved standard slot attention module that explicitly aggregates the perceptual input information for an extra time.

[1] End-to-End Object Detection with Transformers, ECCV2020

[2] Deformable DETR: Deformable Transformers for End-to-End Object Detection, ICLR2021
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
> Strengths

✅ The presented idea is very simple and easy to follow.

✅ It seems that this work is the first one to successfully apply the k-means and the mean-shift algorithm to slot attention-based approach.

✅ The authors provide complete implementations and the code is very clean and easy to read.


> Weaknesses

❎ Some important details are missed:

- In the left of Figure 1, what does it mean with "IF N==1"?

- According to Section 4.1, the authors said "the cluster number is set to M = 2K except for the mean-shift, direct and shared MLPs versions which require M = K". The authors should study the influence
of using different clustering numbers to verify whether the proposed approach is robust to the hyperparameters.

- Why does the model need to be trained "1000 epochs with a warm-up training strategy (Goyal et al., 2017) and an exponential learning rate decay"? Is this a standard training schedule?

- In Table 1, the authors should clearly explain why the k-means (shared MLP) achieves the worst performance.

- According to the provided implementation of [GaussianMeanShift](https://github.com/slot-initialization/linosic/blob/master/slot_attention/model.py#L43), there exist
several hyperparameters including **epsilon** and **sigma**. The authors should also ablate the influence of these hyperparameter choices.


❎ The proposed method seems STRAIGHTFORWARD & LACKS NOVELTY. According to Figure 1, we can see that the critical contribution is applying the k-means scheme or mean-shift scheme to
improve the initialization of the slot representations. Although it seems that this work might be the first to apply a mean-shift scheme for slot initialization, the authors fail to
provide convincing adaptive improvements for the specific problem, thus just verifying that mean-shift is a very powerful tool. Besides, the authors fail to verify the difference between explicitly applying mean-shift and stacking more slot attention modules, which
also aggregate the input representations dynamically.

❎ The authors should provide comparisons to the recent state-of-the-art methods instead of simply reporting some ablation experiment results.

❎ The authors only verify the proposed approach on the very toy benchmarks like CLEVR-Easy, CLEVR-Hard, and CLEVR-Tex.
It would be great if the authors could extend the approach to some real-world benchmarks following very recent works such as SAVi[1] and SAVi++[2]. Especially, according to SAVi++[2], **"the initialization may be learned in an unconditional setting (i.e., learn the initial slot states) or obtained by conditioning the initial state on high-level cues such as bounding boxes of objects of interest in the first video frame"** and the authors also present strong results under unconditional settings. So the authors are encouraged to discuss whether the proposed approach can be applied to a real-world benchmark such as the Waymo Open validation set and analyze whether a complicated initialization is really necessary.

[1] SlotFormer: Unsupervised Visual Dynamics Simulation with Object-Centric Models

[2] SAVi++: Towards End-to-End Object-Centric Learning from Real-World Videos

content.summary_of_the_review:
Designing a better initialization scheme is very important for the success of deep-learning models. This work attempts to present a better initialization scheme for object-centric representation learning. The proposed method is interesting and seems to work very well across various tasks. However, many important details and ablation experiments are required to fully verify the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

According to my previous review experience, this paper presents some encouraging results but lacks lots of details, thus lagging behind the bar of acceptance of ICLR. Indeed, I am not an expert on this track. So, I would like to hear the comments from other reviewers to better justify whether this paper should be accepted.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a method for initializing slot-based unsupervised object-centric models that could help model learning in unsupervised object discovery and novel view synthesis. The authors take the idea of clustering the image features first before passing them into soft-clustering or iterative refining modules (e.g., slot-attention or iodine) to facilitate unsupervised model learning. The authors also proposed to use mean-shift clustering as a way for slot initialization that could generate a variable number of slots. Experiments were conducted on three synthetic datasets and the proposed module shows consistent improvement when being added to slot attention and iodine.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
[+] This paper proposes to start from the initialization perspective of slot-based methods and propose an easy-to-use module for improving model performance in unsupervised object-centric learning. 

[+] The idea of leveraging an additional clustering operation on extracted image feature maps for initializing later soft-clustering/iterative refinement modules are new and show potential as a general way to improve model performance. 

[+] The proposed mean-shift variant of initialization shares similar insights from previous works (e.g. Genesis-v2) and complement existing slot-based methods on the flexibility in the number of slots.

[-] One major concern of this paper lies in the clustering of feature maps before passing this initialization into soft-clustering/iterative refinement modules. The debate here is that good overall performance relies on a good feature map that could generate meaningful cluster centers; however, if the cluster centers are already good enough, then we do not have to pass them into future iterative refinement procedures. As the current experimental results (from tab.1) show only a slight improvement on several synthetic datasets (which are treated as simple tasks compared with other datasets like MOVI, CLEVR-Tex, or real-world scenarios), it is still not clear what this initialization guarantees.

[-] Following this line of thought, the current pipeline benefits iterative refinements with good feature maps; however, this will be hard for complex natural scenes (e.g., real-world scenes or complex textured datasets like CLEVR-Tex) where feature maps are hard to learn. In such cases, it is not clear how well can the clustering algorithm perform (especially with the curse of dimensionality for KDE to break down in mean-shift) and how it will affect the result of the later refinement procedure. 

[-] For models like slot-attention, the iterative refinement shares the same function as the slot-update module except for the choice of clustering function. As the authors from [1] also tried a K-means version (using dot-product score) of the model that showed inferior results compared to slot attention, it is not clear what additional insight this additional clustering procedure provides into the slot-attention module for improving its performance. This lead to more questions like will iterative clustering alone work? can any clustering methods be used? can slot-attention be used for initializing another slot-attn procedure (not parameter sharing)? I'm curious about the authors' thoughts on these.

[-] As it is commonly known that unsupervised object-centric models that require iterative refinement are oftentimes unstable during training, the authors might want to provide a summary of multiple experimental trials to make a more solid comparison, especially given the slight quantitative increase (e.g., from 96% to 99%).

[-] Finally, I guess one minor issue is with the design choice. I somewhat disagree with the authors in removing the learnable parameters for slot initialization. Even with the original gaussian sampling method, the model could potentially use the distribution of slot initialization to reflect the latent distribution of the datasets. These representations, in addition to feature extractors, could potentially serve as pivots that could be generalizable information when transferred to other datasets. The current clustering initialization seems to have destroyed this property and removed potential dataset-level statistics that used to be easily obtained with the vanilla initialization like in slot-attention.

Other questions:
- It seems that the proposed model seems to fit with IODINE than slot attention. Are there any insights on this?
- As the authors stated in the paper, the proposed clustering will also be limited by the computation power given its efficiency. Is there an estimate on the limit of image size or resolution that the current model can handle? and how time efficient is the current model compared with the vanilla ones? will it be significantly slower?
- How to determine the window size of the mean-shift algorithm (i.e., for calculating local means)?

[1] Locatello et al., "Object-Centric Learning with Slot Attention", NeurIPS 2020

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work surveys initialization strategies for slot-based representation learning methods. It evaluates three popular existing methods (Slot Attention, IODINE, uORF) with a few initialization schemes on three standard datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Evaluation of three popular existing methods with several variants of slot initialization on three standard datasets. Variety of empirical results.
- The proposed Mean Shift initialization does not require a fixed number of slots in advance.

Weaknessses:
- A major concern about the proposed strategy is that it shifts the burden from designing good learning algorithms (beyond Slot Attention/IODINE) to searching over the space of possible initializations. The benefit of Slot Attention and IODINE was that they employed learning as well as test-time inference to decompose an image. But the proposed method emphasizes the use of a nonparameteric, non learning-based algorithm. It leaves less room for good representations/segmentations to emerge and for learning to do the job (as suggested by Table 2).
- It’s hard to guess how general the improvements are. 
- The figures are pretty hard to read in general. For example: 
  - Figure 4 contains at least two subfigures.
  - Figure 6 should ideally intersperse input images and segmentations. 
  - Figures 7-12: it’s hard to tell whether the colored rectangles are vectors or matrices.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The structure of the paper could definitely be improved. The flow of ideas could also be smoother. Here are some concrete suggestions:
1. Why abbreviate Slot Attention as SL? Surely SA would be better?
2. Section 2.2: the first paragraph gives the impression that the Pseudoweights are the same as the positional encodings $p_k$. But in fact, the pseudoweights $w_{k,m}$ are defined later. Could you please rewrite to introduce the positional encodings separately from the psudoweights?
3. Equation 3: given that the cluster centers ($c_1$, …, $c_M$) are constant with respect to the slots ($z_1$, … $z_K$), why not drop the k subscript from $c_{k,m}$?
4. Table 1 needs to have a self-contained caption. Please add the full forms of all abbreviations.
content.summary_of_the_review:
My overall score is 4. It is based on (a) concerns about the overall strategy and generality of the proposed method, (b) the quality of the writing.

I have the following questions about the work:
1. Could you please __assess__ the Mean Shift-assigned slot initializations __without further refinement__ (i.e. iteration 0 using IODINE or Slot Attention)? I’m concerned the slot initialization anchors the model on an object too quickly, leaving little room for learning or inference to improve results post-initialization. In other words, the benefits are due to Mean Shift clustering alone, rather than slot initializations being valuable and complementary for Slot Attention/IODINE. It would help if you could add the following to Table 2: Iter 0 results, ARI scores, and Slot Attention in addition to IODINE.
2. Clarifications:
    - __K-means as baseline__: to compute perceptual features for K-means, do you add positional encodings to the image before passing them through a CNN? Surely that would help?
    - __Differentiable Mean Shift__: could you please cite exactly what method you’re referring to in Section 2.3? Also, Algorithm 2 does not suggest you’re using a fully differentiable implementation of Mean Shift. Please clarify.
    - Section 4, Baselines: if `SL + kmeans (direct)` maps cluster centers directly to slots, and `SL + kmeans (shared MLPs)` uses a shared MLP to map the cluster centers, what does `SL + kmeans` do? There’s no details on this.
3. Slot initialization is purely a bottom-up way to promote object discovery. Is there a way to reconcile it with __top-down influence__ (e.g. slots from memory or another context)?

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to initialize the slot attention with k-means clustering and tune the clustering with the mean-shift algorithm. It well-analyzes the current shortcomings of slot attention. The k-means and mean-shift algorithm plugged into slot-attention and IODINE are proven to be effective on various object-centric learning datasets. Complex scenes in CHAIRS also show promising results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strength
1. The idea of utilizing an unsupervised clustering algorithm (i.e., k-means) to boost slot attention and other object-centric learning algorithms is intuitive, especially for the model that relies heavily on initialization. The experimental results also demonstrate such a design can efficiently improve the results on several datasets, including a complex one. 
2. The mean-shift clustering can automatically tune the cluster numbers, which helps to address the problem of tuning the cluster numbers.
3. The experimental results show it can improve both the slot-attention and IODINE with a certain scale, demonstrating such a method could potentially be a plug-in module for more object-centric models.

# Weakness
1. Although the method design and implementation are reasonable to me, it appears more like a marginal improvement to the existing methods without addressing the limitations from the model perspective. 
2. The k-means itself is already a clustering algorithm with its own initialization, stacking it into the slot-attention seems more like an engineering effort, which makes the contribution not sound enough. Intuitively, by iteratively stacking or cascaded design, the model performance can be generally improved within a certain margin.
3. The experiments are performed on three datasets that slot-attention can already behave well with a high ARI. In my experience with slot-attention, it suffers more from the scenes with complex objects and textures, rather than the number of objects. I would like to see the proposed model can address this more significant problem of slot-attention, which limits it from wider applications. I encourage the author to try 1-2 real datasets to see whether they can also apply to real images, which is more convincing.
4. I think a comparison with directly using mean-shift learned feature to learn the reconstruction is needed to analyze how much contribution does the object-centric models (slot attention, IODINE) really make.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
# Clarity
The paper is well-written and I can understand its points clearly.

# Quality and Novelty
The quality is good but the novelty is in lack. Applying such object-centric models to wider scenarios and maybe enable them with new capabilities are more novel to me. The current design is kind of incremental.

# Reproducibility
The author provide the code to implement the method. I did not run it but I believe it is reproducable.
content.summary_of_the_review: My primary concern is the novelty of the paper and the lack of certain experiments as listed in *weakness* and *novelty*. The current contributions of this paper are not sound enough from my perspective.
